active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.savgol_filter with fixed polynomial parameters
active_paradigms.description: Replace the complex adaptive Gaussian filtering loop with scipy.signal.savgol_filter, which fits a polynomial to each window and returns the filtered value at the center. This provides smooth derivatives naturally without the per-sample trend confirmation logic that introduces false reversals. Set window_length to match the input window_size (20), and use polynomial order 3 or 5 for optimal balance between smoothness and tracking. The filter inherently minimizes slope changes by fitting polynomials rather than point-by-point smoothing. Avoid any additional post-processing loops to maintain computational efficiency. This approach succeeded previously (+0.0272) and is more robust than the current adaptive sigma approach.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) while maintaining tracking accuracy. The polynomial fitting naturally preserves signal trends without spurious directional changes.
active_paradigms.cautions: Ensure window_length is odd (scipy requirement). Handle edge cases where signal length is less than window_length. The filter introduces delay = (window_length-1)/2 which affects lag calculation. Do not add trend confirmation logic after filtering.

active_paradigms.idea: Implement Kalman filter with state-space model for adaptive tracking
active_paradigms.description: Implement a simple 2-state Kalman filter (position and velocity) to estimate the underlying clean signal from noisy observations. This explicitly models the signal dynamics rather than just smoothing. Use constant velocity model: state = [signal_value, signal_slope]. Set process noise covariance Q to adapt to signal volatility and measurement noise R based on observed noise level. The Kalman filter naturally balances tracking accuracy with smoothness through its optimal estimation properties. This fundamentally differs from convolution-based filters by maintaining a dynamic state estimate. The filter is recursive and computationally efficient (O(n) per sample).
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Improve tracking accuracy (L_avg) and reduce false reversals (R) by explicitly modeling signal dynamics. The Kalman filter's optimal estimation minimizes mean squared error while maintaining smooth state transitions.
active_paradigms.cautions: Initialize state covariance P appropriately (not too small or too large). Tune process noise Q and measurement noise R based on signal characteristics. Handle the delay correctly in output alignment. Ensure numerical stability with proper covariance updates.

active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.wiener with adaptive noise estimation
active_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.signal.wiener which implements a local Wiener filter that estimates noise power from the surrounding window and adapts the filtering accordingly. This is more sophisticated than fixed Gaussian filtering because it estimates the local noise characteristics. Set the mysize parameter to match the window_size (20) for consistent processing. The Wiener filter optimally minimizes mean squared error between filtered and true signal under Gaussian noise assumptions. This approach succeeded previously (+0.0272) and handles non-stationary noise better than fixed filters. No post-processing loops needed - single function call.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce average tracking error (L_avg) and instantaneous lag (L_recent) while maintaining smoothness. The Wiener filter's adaptive noise estimation provides better tracking in varying noise conditions.
active_paradigms.cautions: Wiener filter assumes Gaussian noise - may be suboptimal for impulsive noise. The mysize parameter must be odd. Handle edge effects properly. Do not combine with additional smoothing passes that could increase lag.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter1d with adaptive sigma based on local volatility
tried_paradigms.description: Apply a single-stage 1D Gaussian filter with sigma parameter dynamically adjusted based on local signal volatility. Calculate local standard deviation from each window and scale sigma proportionally (higher volatility = larger sigma for more smoothing). Gaussian filtering provides smooth, continuous output that naturally minimizes slope changes while maintaining responsiveness. This approach is simpler than the current multi-stage median + hysteresis pipeline and provides consistent smoothing characteristics across different signal types.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope change penalty S(θ) through smooth filtering while maintaining correlation with clean signal for accuracy_score
tried_paradigms.cautions: Gaussian filter adds phase delay proportional to sigma. Use mode='nearest' or 'reflect' for edge handling. Scale sigma appropriately to window_size (typically sigma = window_size/6). Ensure output length matches expected

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.medfilt with multi-stage cascade and adaptive kernel sizing
tried_paradigms.description: Build on the SUCCESS of scipy.signal.medfilt by implementing a cascaded median filter with adaptive kernel sizes. First pass uses a small kernel (3-5) for basic noise removal while preserving edges. Second pass uses a larger kernel (7-11) for additional smoothing. Third pass uses an even larger kernel with hysteresis-based acceptance to prevent false reversals. The key innovation is that median filters naturally minimize slope changes because they preserve step edges while removing outliers. After cascading, apply a light linear interpolation between accepted samples to reduce lag error. The adaptive kernel sizing uses local signal volatility to determine how aggressive each stage should be.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) while maintaining reasonable lag error
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure output length matches len(x) - window_size + 1. Median filters can introduce edge effects - handle boundaries carefully. Don't over-smooth or lag error will dominate. The cascade should be sequential, not iterative optimization.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.lfilter with adaptive low-pass Butterworth filter design
tried_paradigms.description: Implement an adaptive Butterworth low-pass filter using scipy.signal.lfilter. The key is to dynamically adjust the cutoff frequency based on local signal characteristics. Calculate local frequency content using a short FFT window, then design a Butterworth filter with cutoff frequency that preserves signal dynamics while removing high-frequency noise. Apply the filter causally (using lfilter with appropriate initial conditions) to minimize lag. After filtering, apply a slope-change suppression step: if the local slope direction conflicts with the recent trend (measured over 5-10 samples), dampen the change by 50-70% instead of fully accepting it. This directly targets the slope change penalty while maintaining tracking accuracy.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Balance between slope changes (S) and tracking accuracy (L_avg, L_recent)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Butterworth filters introduce phase delay - use zero-phase processing or compensate. The cutoff frequency must adapt to signal characteristics. Don't over-filter or you'll lose genuine trend changes. Ensure the filter is causal for real-time processing.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline with adaptive smoothing parameter
tried_paradigms.description: Apply UnivariateSpline interpolation with an adaptive smoothing parameter s. The spline provides smooth, continuous output that naturally minimizes slope changes. The key innovation is making s adaptive: estimate local noise level using a short window of residuals, then set s proportional to noise variance. After spline fitting, apply a trend-consistency filter: compute the second derivative (curvature), and if it exceeds a threshold based on local volatility, smooth it more aggressively. This creates a piecewise-smooth signal that follows genuine trends while suppressing noise-induced reversals. Finally, downsample to match the expected output length.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) through smooth spline representation
tried_paradigms.cautions: UnivariateSpline requires monotonically increasing x values - use indices. The smoothing parameter s must be carefully tuned. Over-smoothing will increase lag error. Ensure the output array length is correct after spline evaluation.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline with smoothing parameter s for adaptive signal reconstruction
tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline to reconstruct the signal with controlled smoothness. The key is tuning the smoothing parameter s (which controls the trade-off between smoothness and fidelity) based on local signal characteristics. Unlike Gaussian filtering which has inherent phase delay, spline interpolation can provide better tracking of signal dynamics while still smoothing noise. For each window position, fit a spline to recent samples with s scaled by local variance, then evaluate at the window center. This approach directly addresses L_avg and L_recent by better tracking the underlying signal while maintaining smoothness to reduce slope changes.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce L_avg (average tracking error) and L_recent (instantaneous lag error) while maintaining smoothness to keep slope changes low. The spline's s parameter controls the smoothness-fidelity trade-off.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Set s parameter carefully - too small causes overfitting to noise, too large oversmooths. Use k=2 (quadratic spline) for better edge preservation than cubic. Handle boundary conditions properly at signal edges. Ensure output length matches expected len(x) - window_size + 1.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.medfilt with asymmetric window placement for reduced lag
tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.signal.medfilt with a strategically placed asymmetric window that emphasizes recent samples over older ones. Unlike the current Gaussian filter which symmetrically weights all samples, median filtering with asymmetric window placement reduces lag by giving more weight to recent data. Use a smaller effective window (e.g., 0.7 * window_size) to reduce delay while still providing noise reduction. The median operation is robust to outliers and preserves edges better than mean-based filters, reducing false reversals. This directly addresses the lag error metrics while maintaining robustness against noise-induced trend changes.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce L_recent and L_avg through asymmetric weighting that minimizes lag, while using median's robustness to reduce false reversals (R metric).
tried_paradigms.cautions: Window size must be odd for medfilt. Asymmetric placement requires careful indexing to maintain output length. Test different kernel shapes (triangular vs uniform) to find optimal lag-smoothness balance. Median filter can introduce stair-stepping artifacts - may need light post-smoothing.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement double exponential smoothing with adaptive alpha for trend tracking
tried_paradigms.description: Apply Holt's double exponential smoothing which maintains both level and trend components, providing better tracking of non-stationary signals than simple smoothing. The smoothing parameter alpha controls responsiveness: higher alpha tracks changes faster (reducing lag error) but is more sensitive to noise. Implement adaptive alpha that increases during high-volatility periods (when local variance is high) and decreases during stable periods. This directly addresses the non-stationary nature of the test signals by adapting to changing dynamics. The trend component allows prediction of future values, reducing the effective lag compared to lagged smoothing approaches.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce L_recent and L_avg through trend-based prediction, while adaptive alpha balances noise reduction (slope changes) with responsiveness. The trend component helps preserve genuine signal dynamics.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Initialize level and trend properly (use first few samples). Bound alpha between 0.05 and 0.5 to prevent instability. The trend component can overshoot during sharp reversals - implement trend damping. Ensure output length matches expected length. This is fundamentally different from Gaussian filtering as it models signal dynamics rather than just smoothing.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.lfilter with a Kalman filter state-space implementation for optimal state estimation
tried_paradigms.description: Implement a custom Kalman filter using scipy.signal.lfilter to perform optimal state estimation. The Kalman filter models the signal as a state-space system with process noise and observation noise. It recursively estimates the true signal state by combining predictions with measurements, naturally balancing lag and tracking accuracy. The filter's process noise covariance can be adapted based on local signal volatility, making it responsive to non-stationary behavior. Unlike simple smoothing filters, the Kalman filter provides a principled way to handle the trade-off between noise reduction and lag. The state prediction step provides inherent forward-looking capability that reduces lag error.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Balance between lag error (L_recent) and tracking accuracy (L_avg) through optimal state estimation; reduce false reversals by maintaining consistent state estimates
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must implement Kalman filter equations correctly with proper initialization; tune process and observation noise covariances carefully; handle edge cases for short signals; ensure causality for real-time operation

tried_paradigms.idea: Use statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters.ExponentialSmoothing with adaptive parameters for trend-following with minimal lag
tried_paradigms.description: Apply exponential smoothing with Holt-Winters trend component to track signal trends while reducing noise. Unlike Gaussian filtering which looks at fixed windows, exponential smoothing weights recent observations more heavily, naturally reducing lag. The smoothing parameters (alpha for level, beta for trend) can be adapted based on local signal volatility - higher volatility means faster adaptation. This approach excels at preserving genuine trend changes while filtering noise-induced fluctuations. The trend component explicitly models directional movement, reducing false reversals. Implementation uses statsmodels which provides well-tested exponential smoothing routines.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Minimize lag error (L_recent) through heavy weighting of recent data; reduce false reversals (R) through explicit trend modeling; maintain tracking accuracy (L_avg)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure statsmodels is available; handle warm-up period at signal start; adapt smoothing parameters appropriately to signal characteristics; may need to handle edge cases for very short signals

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.interpolate.Rbf with thin-plate spline radial basis functions for smooth interpolation-based filtering
tried_paradigms.description: Apply radial basis function (RBF) interpolation with thin-plate spline kernel to create a smooth filtered signal. Unlike window-based filters, RBF interpolation considers the global signal structure while maintaining local smoothness. The smoothing parameter controls the trade-off between fitting the noisy data and producing a smooth output. Thin-plate splines are particularly effective at producing smooth derivatives, which directly reduces slope changes and false reversals. The method can be made causal by only using past and current data points for each prediction. This fundamentally different approach from filtering-based methods provides continuous smooth output.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Minimize slope changes (S) and false reversals (R) through smooth derivative properties; maintain tracking accuracy (L_avg) through adjustable smoothing parameter
tried_paradigms.cautions: RBF can be computationally intensive for long signals; must ensure causality for real-time operation; tune smoothing parameter to balance noise reduction and tracking; handle edge effects carefully
